items.stem: Across period 3 from sodium to chlorine, how does atomic radius change and why?

options.text: It decreases because nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell
options.rationale: Correct: increasing effective nuclear charge pulls the same-shell electrons inward.

options.text: It increases because more electrons are added
options.rationale: Electrons enter the same principal shell, so size does not grow.

options.text: It stays constant across the period
options.rationale: Effective nuclear charge changes, so radius changes.

options.text: It decreases because a new shell is added
options.rationale: No new shell is added within a period.

items.explanation: Correct: increasing effective nuclear charge pulls the same-shell electrons inward.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about the mole concept are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: One mole contains Avogadro's number of entities
options.rationale: Correct: a mole is defined by Avogadro's constant.

options.text: Molar mass in g/mol is numerically equal to the relative formula mass
options.rationale: Correct: this equivalence lets us convert mass to moles.

options.text: One mole of any gas always occupies 1 litre
options.rationale: Molar gas volume depends on temperature and pressure, and is not 1 L.
The mole counts entities; mass depends on molar mass.

items.explanation: Correct: a mole is defined by Avogadro's constant.

items.stem: Why should a chemist not blindly trust a machine-learning solubility prediction?

options.text: The model may extrapolate beyond its training data and give unreliable values
options.rationale: Correct: predictions outside the applicability domain are untrustworthy.

options.text: Models can never be useful in chemistry
options.rationale: Models are useful within their validated domain.
Solubility is readily measured; the issue is model reliability.
No model is exact; validation is required.

items.explanation: Correct: predictions outside the applicability domain are untrustworthy.
